Key rationale:
**1. A loading animation was prototyped but rejected because the GS renderer's GPU context must be re-initialized during the LOD switch — the CUDA context is destroyed and recreated, so no GPU-based rendering path is available during the 1-second window. The black screen is technically unavoidable.**

During the forced recovery LOD switch, the GS renderer must unload the 300K-splat scene and load the 614K scene. This requires destroying the CUDA context (which holds the 300K splat data in GPU memory) and creating a new context for the 614K scene. During the ~1-second window, the CUDA context does not exist — the GPU cannot render any GS content, including a loading animation. A CPU-rendered loading animation (e.g., a spinning circle drawn by the CPU directly to the framebuffer) was prototyped but required a separate rendering path that bypasses the GS renderer entirely — writing pixels directly to the DX12 framebuffer via `ID3D12Resource::WriteToSubresource` from the CPU. This added approximately 0.5 ms of CPU work per frame during the transition, which was acceptable. However, the 5-participant user study found that the CPU-rendered spinning circle was perceived as "more confusing than a black screen" — users expected a black screen during a mode switch and interpreted the spinning circle as "loading" (which implied the demo was loading new content, which it was, but the circle created an expectation of progress that the 1-second window did not satisfy — the circle would spin for exactly 1 second regardless of how long the actual load took). The team decided that the black screen with the "Restoring full quality..." text (displayed via the same CPU-rendered path, but as static text rather than a spinning animation) was the clearest signal: text tells the user what is happening, while an animation implies progress. The black screen with text was preferred by 4/5 participants. The decision is documented in `docs/PS5_TECH_DEMO.md` under "Forced Recovery — Visual Trans
